body:
> When an Autoload (singleton) script is decorated with `@tool` and contains a _draw() function (e.g., for custom 2D rendering), its drawn content appears overlaid on the editor UI itself after restarting the editor.

AFICT this is correct/expected behavior, `@tool` scripts do run in the editor, and autoloaded scenes with `@tool` script attached to the scene root node are instantiated in the editor (and added to the editor SceneTree).

> This did not happen in Godot 4.5, where Autoload scripts with `@tool` and _draw() were correctly ignored in the editor viewport unless explicitly added to the scene tree.

If opening the MRP in v4.5.1.stable.official [f62fdbde1] it errors:
```
  ERROR: Failed to instantiate scene state of "uid://di3q4e78uofm2", node count is 0. Make sure the PackedScene resource is valid.
  ERROR: Failed to create an autoload, path is not pointing to a scene or a script: uid://di3q4e78uofm2.
```
So the drawing not showing in there is caused by the autoload failing to be instantiated because it's stored as uid (which was added in #112193 (merged in 4.6.dev4)).

If in v4.5.1.stable.official [f62fdbde1] you'd remove the autoload and readd it, it would be stored by path, and it would run in the editor as in 4.6, as expected (no need to restart the editor):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e0c74363-e55e-4436-a31a-0c5911d1e284

@timothyqiu Would #113005 resolve this issue / make an autoload scene created in 4.6 be loadable in 4.5?

Thank you for your response.

I understand that, from an engine implementation standpoint, running @tool scripts in the editor and executing _draw() may be "technically consistent." However, there's a serious disconnect between this technical consistency and what users reasonably expect—and that is precisely where the problem lies.

Autoloads are designed to serve as logical singletons, managing game state, configuration, save systems, audio, or other backend logic. When developers add @tool to an Autoload, they typically do so only to:

Inspect or debug exported variables in the Inspector,
Respond to editor signals (e.g., scene changes),
Precompute data during editing.
No one expects their score manager or settings system to suddenly start drawing shapes over the Scene dock, Inspector, or even the Project Manager window!

If custom rendering in the editor UI is needed, Godot already provides the correct mechanism: EditorPlugins. They offer controlled lifecycles, well-defined rendering contexts, and clear boundaries. Allowing ordinary Autoload scripts to pollute the editor viewport not only violates separation of concerns but also blurs the line between game logic and editor tooling.

If this is truly “expected behavior,” then I must ask: What is the design intent behind it?

Is the goal to encourage users to implement editor visuals via Autoloads? If so, why isn’t there accompanying documentation, warnings, or an opt-in mechanism? Why silently introduce visual interference into thousands of existing projects upon upgrade?

More importantly, this behavior introduces real risks:

Visual clutter that obstructs normal editor usage,
New users accidentally triggering drawing just by inheriting from Node2D (e.g., to use _process),
Potential performance overhead or unintended input/event conflicts.
Just because something can run doesn’t mean it should run; just because something can draw doesn’t mean it should draw.

I respectfully urge the team to reconsider this design: by default, Autoload root nodes should not participate in editor viewport rendering. If advanced use cases genuinely require this capability, it should be enabled explicitly—such as via a checkbox in the Autoload settings like “Visible in Editor”—rather than forcing all users to pay the cost for an edge case.

This isn’t just a minor quirk; it’s a meaningful break in user mental models and workflow. I hope it can be treated as a user experience regression and addressed accordingly.

Thank you again for your outstanding work on Godot. 🙏

This is the expected behavior because `autoload` essentially adds nodes to the `/root` in node tree automatically. The Godot editor itself is also a Godot program, and `@tool` scripts simply inform the editor that they can be executed. When these two are combined, a node capable of executing script logic normally is added to the editor.

Not only will `_draw()` execute as expected, but other methods will as well. If you do not want the code in `@tool` scripts to run in the editor, Godot provides the `Engine.is_editor_hint()` method to determine whether the current code is being executed in the editor. For more details, please refer to https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/plugins/running_code_in_the_editor.html.

``` @tool extends Node2D func _draw(): draw_circle(Vector2(100, 100), 50, Color.RED) ``` ``` @tool extends Node2D func _draw(): if !Engine.is_editor_hint(): draw_circle(Vector2(100, 100), 50, Color.RED) ``` The solution is to add `Engine.is_editor_hint()` in `_draw()`. The official documentation already includes tutorials and precautions for using `@tool`. https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/plugins/running_code_in_the_editor.html

Thank you for the response, but I believe there’s a misunderstanding about the actual issue.

I’m not questioning whether @tool scripts run in the editor—that behavior is well-documented and expected.

I’m also not asking how to prevent code from running in the editor—I know about Engine.is_editor_hint() and use it regularly.

The real problem is this:

When an Autoload script (which is a logical singleton, not a visual node) inherits from CanvasItem and contains _draw(), it gets automatically rendered onto the editor’s UI—even though it was never added to any editable scene.

This is not about “code executing.” It’s about unintended visual side effects caused by the engine implicitly treating Autoload root nodes as part of the editor’s viewport rendering tree.

To clarify with an example:

If I create an Autoload like this:
```gdscript

@tool
extends Node2D

# Intended only for visual debugging within the editor's scene view,
# not for rendering onto the editor UI itself.
@export var offset: float = 200:
	set(value):
		offset = value
		queue_redraw()

func _draw():
	draw_circle(Vector2.RIGHT * offset, 50, Color.DARK_GOLDENROD)
```

…then a red circle appears over the Scene dock, Inspector, and even the Project Manager—simply because the Autoload exists.

This violates fundamental design principles:

Autoloads are backend services, not UI elements.
Editor UI customization should be done via EditorPlugins, not game-level singletons.
Rendering should be opt-in, not a hidden side effect of using Node2D + @tool.
The fact that “the editor is a Godot program” doesn’t justify allowing arbitrary game scripts to paint over its interface. By that logic, any @tool script could also intercept mouse input, modify the scene tree, or cause performance issues—and we clearly don’t want that by default.

So again:

✅ Yes, @tool scripts run in the editor — good.

❌ But they should not automatically render in the editor viewport unless explicitly designed to do so (e.g., as an EditorPlugin).

I urge the team to treat this as a usability regression: either exclude Autoload root nodes from editor viewport rendering by default, or add a clear opt-in mechanism. The current behavior breaks user expectations and introduces visual noise into the editing workflow.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

> Autoloads are backend services, not UI elements. 

So why did you set `Autoload` to inherit from `Node2D`? `Node2D` inherits from `CanvasItem`, which is used for drawing visual elements. If you don't want drawing functionality, you should directly use `Node`.

The current mechanism is very clear: `Autoload` will be added to `/root`, and `@tool` will run in the editor. The editor has the same scene tree as the game (the editor itself is largely a Godot game). `Node2D` has drawing functionality, so an `Autoload` marked with `@tool` that inherits from `Node2D` will be added to the editor's `/root` and drawn normally.

```gdscript
@tool
extends Node2D

# Intended only for visual debugging within the editor's scene view,
# not for rendering onto the editor UI itself.
@export var offset: float = 200:
	set(value):
		offset = value
		queue_redraw()

func _draw():
	draw_circle(Vector2.RIGHT * offset, 50, Color.DARK_GOLDENROD)
```

My Autoload is a .tscn scene file, and the script you see above is attached to its root node.

The purpose of this scene is simple: I want to be able to open it directly in the editor and visually debug it—for example, by seeing the circle drawn at the correct offset. That works perfectly when I edit the scene itself.

However, when this same scene is used as an Autoload, something unexpected happens:

it draws not only in the scene viewport (which is fine), but also directly onto the global editor UI—overlaying the Inspector, docks, and even the Project Manager window.

I do need the drawing functionality for visual debugging within scenes, but I absolutely do not expect an Autoload—which exists as a background singleton—to render anything on the editor’s UI just because it inherits from Node2D.

This feels like a context mix-up: the engine treats the Autoload as if it were part of the editor’s main viewport, even though it’s never added to any visible scene tree.

> Autoloads are backend services, not UI elements. Autoloads are **nodes**, added to the root of the scene tree. They behave like any other node added to the tree. They are not "UI elements" or "backend services" or whatever, unless you use them this way. Moreover, it's not a regression. The same "bug" appears in 4.5.1, if the autoload is referenced with a path instead of UID: Closing, as this is expected behavior. Feel free to open a proposal instead. EDIT: If you still have doubts, here is the scene structure of the editor, as seen in EditorDebugger: Your autoload is next to EditorNode, which is the main node of the editor. The documentation already mentions this behavior: (although I guess it doesn't clarify that the autoloads are also added in the editor, but that's documentation issue)
